\begin{document}

\title{PromptGuard: A Browser-Side Prompt Injection Detector and an Evaluation of In-Distribution versus
Cross-Dataset Generalization}

\author{\IEEEauthorblockN{Arshitha S, Charithra H S, Chandrakala Hipparagi}
\IEEEauthorblockA{\todo{affiliation}}}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Prompt injection lets text that a user pastes into a chat assistant, such as an email, a web page or a table,
redirect the model. We present PromptGuard, an open-source browser extension with a self-hostable API that
checks the prompt box of hosted chat services before the text is sent, reports a decomposable risk score
and shows the words behind a flag. We train three detectors on one public dataset (TF-IDF with logistic
regression, DistilBERT and ModernBERT) and compare them with Llama Prompt Guard 2, a ProtectAI detector and
two rule baselines. In distribution the three trained models are statistically tied (binary accuracy
\pgr{3}{pr.models.classical.bootstrap.binary.accuracy.point} for the linear model, McNemar
$p\geq\pgr{2}{pr.pairwise.classical_vs_guard.binary.mcnemar.p_value}$), and the linear model needs
\pgr{1}{pr.models.classical.latency.batch_1.median_ms_per_prompt}~ms per prompt on a CPU. On three other public
datasets their accuracy falls to \extv{\dsx}{guard}{accuracy}--\extv{\dsd}{guard}{accuracy} with
false-positive rates up to \extv{\dsx}{guard}{false_positive_rate}; they flag nearly every clean document
from the BIPIA benchmark, and they flag perturbed benign text as attacks. The published detectors transfer
better across datasets but miss almost every task injection hidden in a document. Test scores on a single
public dataset therefore overstate how useful such detectors are in front of real user text.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
prompt injection, large language models, LLM security, browser extension, text classification, distribution shift
\end{IEEEkeywords}

\section{Introduction}
Prompt injection is the first risk in the OWASP list for LLM applications \cite{owasp2025llm01}. In its
indirect form, the attacking text sits in content that reaches the model on the user's behalf, such as a
web page, an email or a document \cite{greshake2023not}. With chat assistants, the most common way such
content reaches the model is still the simplest one: the user copies it into the prompt box.

PromptGuard is a browser extension that checks the prompt box of hosted chat services before the text is
sent, backed by a small open-source API that anyone can host. This paper describes the system and asks a
question any such tool depends on: is a detector trained on a public prompt-injection dataset good enough
to run in front of real user text? We train three detectors on one public dataset, a TF-IDF logistic
regression, DistilBERT and ModernBERT, and compare them with two published detectors and two rule
baselines in distribution, on three other public datasets, on documents with embedded injections and
under perturbations.

In distribution the three trained models are statistically tied, with accuracy around
\pgr{2}{pr.models.classical.bootstrap.binary.accuracy.point}, and the linear model is by far the cheapest.
Everywhere else they fail: accuracy falls to near chance on two of the three external datasets, nearly every
clean pasted document is flagged, and perturbations of benign text are flagged as attacks. The published
detectors generalize better across datasets but miss most injections hidden in documents. On benign text
from other datasets, the classical model mostly leaves questions alone and flags much of everything else
(Section~\ref{sec:cross}).

Our contributions are:
\begin{itemize}
\item an open-source, browser-side detection system with a self-hostable API that reports a decomposable
risk score and, when no pattern applies, the words behind a flag (Sections~\ref{sec:system}--\ref{sec:data});
\item an evaluation that separates in-distribution accuracy from cross-dataset accuracy, the pasted-document
case and perturbation robustness, with published baselines and confidence intervals (Section~\ref{sec:eval});
\item a negative result with a diagnosis: single-dataset test scores substantially overstate how well such
detectors work in the setting they are meant for.
\end{itemize}
Code, pinned data revisions and the scripts that produce every number in this paper are available at
\url{https://github.com/Arshu-1104/AI-Prompt-Injection} (commit \texttt{\pgnum{git.commit}}).

\section{Related Work}\label{sec:related}
\emph{Attacks.} Perez and Ribeiro showed goal hijacking and prompt leaking with hand-written prompts
\cite{perez2022ignore}, and Greshake et al.\ moved the payload into third-party content that an
application retrieves, the indirect setting we target \cite{greshake2023not}. Later work studied
injection against deployed applications \cite{liu2023promptinjection}, separated out jailbreaks
\cite{liu2023jailbreaking}, hid instructions inside larger benign tasks \cite{jiang2023packer}, and
searched for injections automatically \cite{zhang2024goal,pasquini2024neural}. Susceptibility differs
across model families \cite{benjamin2024systematically}. Liu et al.\ formalized attacks and defenses in one
benchmark \cite{liu2024formalizing}, and BIPIA collects indirect injections in emails, tables and other
documents \cite{yi2025bipia}; we use its documents and attack sentences in Section~\ref{sec:eval}.

\emph{Detectors.} Llama Guard classifies prompts and responses against a safety taxonomy
\cite{inan2023llamaguard}; Prompt Guard 2 is a small mDeBERTa classifier for injection and jailbreak
intent \cite{meta2025promptguard2}; PromptShield evaluates detectors under deployment conditions
\cite{jacob2025promptshield}; and Attention Tracker detects injection from the attention of the target
model itself \cite{hung2024attention}. InjecGuard measures over-defense, i.e.\ benign prompts flagged for
looking like attacks \cite{li2024injecguard}, and fine-tuned detectors can be broken by adaptive attacks
\cite{pandya2025attention}. Baseline defenses such as perplexity filtering trade detection for
benign-task performance \cite{jain2023baseline}. PromptLocate localizes the injected span instead of
classifying the whole input \cite{jia2026promptlocate}. Defending a production model needs several layers
once retrieval and tools are involved \cite{shi2025gemini}, and injection reaches LLM judges and tool
selection \cite{shi2024judge,shi2025toolselection} as well as specialised applications such as resume
screening \cite{mu2025resume}.

\emph{This work.} PromptGuard is not a new detector architecture. It places a detector in the user's
browser, in front of any hosted chat service, and asks how far detectors trained on one public dataset
carry to others. The name is unrelated to Meta's Prompt Guard models \cite{meta2025promptguard2}, which
we use as a baseline.

\section{System and Threat Model}\label{sec:system}

\subsection{Components}
PromptGuard has three parts (Fig.~\ref{fig:arch}). A Chrome extension watches the prompt box on
chatgpt.com, chat.openai.com, claude.ai and gemini.google.com. When the user has stopped typing for
\pgnum{e2e.config.debounce_ms}~ms, it sends the text in the box to a REST API and draws a badge next to
the box. The API runs one of the detectors of Section~\ref{sec:data} and returns a label, a confidence,
a risk score, the attack patterns that matched and, when no pattern explains a flag, the words that
contributed most to it. A web dashboard issues API keys with a per-key rate limit, shows request logs and
has a playground for manual tests (Fig.~\ref{fig:explain}). The code is open source, and the API and
dashboard can be self-hosted.

The detectors use three labels, SAFE, SUSPICIOUS and MALICIOUS, which the extension shows as Safe,
Review and Danger. We use the first set throughout. Since the training data has no SUSPICIOUS class of
its own (Section~\ref{sec:data}), our headline metric is binary: SAFE against not SAFE.

\subsection{Threat model}
Two different attacks are often both called prompt injection, and a tool in the user's browser helps
against only one of them.

\emph{Jailbreaks.} The user writes the adversarial prompt, to make the model ignore its own rules. The
user is the attacker and controls the browser, so a client-side detector is no security control here:
it can be switched off. Jailbreaks are part of our training and test data and we report how well they
are detected, but we make no protection claim for them.

\emph{Indirect injection.} The adversarial text comes from a third party, in an email, a web page, a
document or a table, and the user pastes it into the chat together with their own request
\cite{greshake2023not}. The user is the victim. The extension sees the pasted text before it reaches the
model and can warn the user. This is the case PromptGuard targets. The attacker controls the pasted
content, including its wording, but not the extension, the API or the user's own request. Content that
the chat service fetches by itself, such as web results, uploaded files or tool outputs, never passes
through the prompt box and is out of scope, as are agents with tool access \cite{willison2025trifecta}.
Section~\ref{sec:eval} tests this case with injections embedded in pasted documents.

\subsection{Privacy}
While it is enabled and configured, the extension sends the prompt-box text, the API key and the chosen
model to the configured endpoint and nowhere else. The API stores a SHA-256 hash of the text, the label,
scores, matched patterns, latency, model and key; the text itself is stored only if this is turned on
for the key, which it is not by default. An unsalted hash of a short or common prompt can be guessed, so
users who need more than this can self-host the API. The extension keeps the API key in local, unsynced
extension storage, asks for host permission only for the hosted API and, when the user saves another
endpoint, for that one origin, and contains no remote code or analytics.

\section{Data and Models}\label{sec:data}

\subsection{Training data}
We train and select models on the neuralchemy prompt-injection dataset \cite{neuralchemy2025} at a
pinned revision and use its official splits: \pgnum{pr.dataset.source_rows.train} training,
\pgnum{pr.dataset.source_rows.validation} validation and \pgnum{pr.dataset.source_rows.test} test rows,
each labelled benign or malicious. To train the SUSPICIOUS class we derive it inside each split, after
splitting: \pgp{0}{meta.build.suspicious_fraction_of_safe}\% of the SAFE rows get an appended manipulation
phrase, and a small set of hand-written suspicious prompts is assigned to exactly one split by a hash of
its text. Leetspeak variants of \pgp{0}{meta.build.evasion_augment_fraction}\% of the MALICIOUS rows and
benign hard negatives are added the same way. Any derived row whose normalized text also occurs in
another split is dropped, and so is any training row that matches an evaluation row; official
evaluation rows are never dropped. The processed splits have \pgnum{pr.dataset.processed.train.rows},
\pgnum{pr.dataset.processed.validation.rows} and \pgnum{pr.dataset.processed.test.rows} rows. Because
SUSPICIOUS is synthetic, every headline number is binary and computed on the
\pgnum{pr.models.classical.runs.0.binary.n_samples} original test rows with their original labels.

\subsection{Detectors}
\emph{Classical.} TF-IDF features of word 1--3-grams and within-word character 2--5-grams feed a
multinomial logistic regression with balanced class weights. Among \pgnum{trn.classical_model.validation.n_keys}
candidates (logistic regression with four regularization strengths on word or word-plus-character
features, a random forest and multinomial naive Bayes), we keep the one with the highest weighted F1 on
the validation split: word-plus-character features with $C=1$ (validation F1
\pgr{4}{trn.classical_model.validation.logreg_word+char_C_1.three_class.f1_weighted}; the runner-up scores
\pgr{4}{trn.classical_model.validation.logreg_word+char_C_10.three_class.f1_weighted}). The fit is
deterministic, so all seeds give the same model.

\emph{Transformers.} We fine-tune DistilBERT (\texttt{distilbert-base-uncased}, ``bert'') and ModernBERT-base
(``guard'') for \pgnum{bert42.hyperparameters.epochs} epochs at learning rate
\pgsci{bert42.hyperparameters.learning_rate} with inputs truncated to \pgnum{bert42.hyperparameters.max_length}
tokens, batch sizes \pgnum{bert42.hyperparameters.batch_size} and \pgnum{guard42.hyperparameters.batch_size},
over \pgnum{pr.models.bert.summary.n_seeds_ok} and \pgnum{pr.models.guard.summary.n_seeds_ok} seeds.

\emph{Risk score.} The API reports $R=\min(100,\max(0,\,b+\min(4m,15)+20(c-0.5)))$, where $b$ is 15, 55
or 85 for SAFE, SUSPICIOUS or MALICIOUS, $m$ is the number of matched patterns and $c$ the model's
confidence (its largest class probability). The patterns explain a result but never change the label.
The API returns the three terms with the score.

\emph{Rule floor and escalation.} Two rules sit on top of the classical model. A chat-template token
(such as \texttt{<|im\_start|>}) or text hidden entirely in tags raises SAFE to SUSPICIOUS. When the guard
model is loaded, a classical SUSPICIOUS verdict with confidence below 0.65 is replaced by the guard
model's verdict. We evaluate both rules in Section~\ref{sec:eval}.

\section{Evaluation}\label{sec:eval}

\subsection{Setup}
All models are scored as published or as trained, without tuning on any evaluation set. Inputs pass
through the same normalization as the API. We report binary accuracy, false-positive rate (FPR) and
threshold-free AUROC, with 95\% confidence intervals from 1000 bootstrap resamples of the evaluation set;
for small groups we give Wilson intervals instead. Paired comparisons on the same rows use an exact
McNemar test. Baselines are ProtectAI's DeBERTa-v3 detector \cite{protectai2024deberta} and Llama Prompt
Guard 2 \cite{meta2025promptguard2}, used as published (their benign and attack labels map to SAFE and
MALICIOUS), plus two rule baselines: our regular expressions alone (any match is an attack) and a fixed
keyword list. Latency is CPU time per prompt at batch size 1 on an \pgnum{pr.environment.latency_machine.cpu_model}.

\subsection{In distribution}
On the original test rows (Table~\ref{tab:indist}) the three trained models are statistically tied: the
classical model and DistilBERT differ by
\pgr{4}{pr.pairwise.classical_vs_bert.binary.difference} in accuracy (McNemar
$p=\pgr{2}{pr.pairwise.classical_vs_bert.binary.mcnemar.p_value}$), and the classical model and ModernBERT
by \pgr{4}{pr.pairwise.classical_vs_guard.binary.difference}
($p=\pgr{2}{pr.pairwise.classical_vs_guard.binary.mcnemar.p_value}$). The classical model needs a fraction
of the CPU time. ProtectAI's detector is less accurate here (McNemar
$p=\pgsci{pr.pairwise.classical_vs_protectai.binary.mcnemar.p_value}$ against the classical model), mainly
because it misses attacks: its true-positive rate is
\pgr{3}{cur.sets.\testset.protectai.fixed_operating_point.tpr} against
\pgr{3}{cur.sets.\testset.classical.fixed_operating_point.tpr} for the classical model. The regular
expressions match only a few attacks; most attacks in this dataset are obfuscated or reworded.

\subsection{Across datasets}\label{sec:cross}
Table~\ref{tab:cross} applies the same models, without retraining, to three public test sets:
xTRam1 \cite{xtram1safeguard}, deepset \cite{deepsetpromptinjections} (English and German) and Qualifire
\cite{qualifirebenchmark}. Texts that also occur in our training data were removed first; none did.

All three trained models fall to near chance. On xTRam1 their accuracy is between
\extv{\dsx}{guard}{accuracy} and \extv{\dsx}{bert}{accuracy}, and they flag between
\extv{\dsx}{bert}{false_positive_rate} and \extv{\dsx}{guard}{false_positive_rate} of the benign prompts; on
Qualifire they reach at most \extv{\dsq}{bert}{accuracy}. Their AUROC lies between
\extv{\dsx}{bert}{auroc.auroc} and \extv{\dsd}{bert}{auroc.auroc}, so no threshold separates the classes well.
A threshold chosen on our validation split does not close the gap either: for the classical model on
Qualifire it moves accuracy from \extv{\dsq}{classical}{accuracy} to
\extv{\dsq}{classical}{validation_tuned.accuracy}. The in-distribution tie between the classical model and
the transformers (Table~\ref{tab:indist}) therefore says nothing about which one generalizes; none of them does.

ProtectAI's detector does much better on xTRam1 (accuracy \extv{\dsx}{protectai}{accuracy}) and Qualifire
(\extv{\dsq}{protectai}{accuracy}). Its training data is only partly disclosed, so part of this gap may be
overlap with these sets. The simple rule baselines are also informative: on xTRam1 and Qualifire the keyword list is more accurate
(\extv{\dsx}{keyword}{accuracy} and \extv{\dsq}{keyword}{accuracy}) than any model we trained. It is not a
good detector, since it finds few attacks (its AUROC is at most \extv{\dsx}{keyword}{auroc.auroc}); it
simply almost never flags a benign prompt, which is where the trained models lose most.

What do the false positives have in common? With a simple, documented heuristic for sentence form, the
benign external prompts that the classical model flags are rarely questions: on xTRam1,
\pgr{2}{diag.external_true_safe.\dsx.false_positives.question.share} of them are questions against
\pgr{2}{diag.external_true_safe.\dsx.true_negatives.question.share} of the benign prompts it leaves alone,
and on Qualifire \pgr{2}{diag.external_true_safe.\dsq.false_positives.question.share} against
\pgr{2}{diag.external_true_safe.\dsq.true_negatives.question.share}. In the training data, questions are more
common among benign rows than among attacks (\pgr{2}{diag.training.SAFE.question.share} against
\pgr{2}{diag.training.MALICIOUS.question.share}), while imperatives are common in both
(\pgr{2}{diag.training.SAFE.imperative.share} and \pgr{2}{diag.training.MALICIOUS.imperative.share}). The
model therefore behaves as if a question were evidence of safety, and benign text in other forms, such as
the task instructions that fill xTRam1, is flagged.

\subsection{Injections in pasted documents}
Table~\ref{tab:docs} uses the threat model's case: \pgnum{docs.counts.documents.email} emails and
\pgnum{docs.counts.documents.table} tables from BIPIA \cite{yi2025bipia}, framed with BIPIA's question as a
user would paste them, once clean and once with a BIPIA attack sentence at the start, middle or end. Most
BIPIA attacks ask for an unrelated task (``Recommend a good book'') rather than overriding instructions;
a second variant adds ``Ignore all previous instructions.'' in front of the same sentence.

The three models we trained flag nearly every clean document: the FPR is \docfpr{classical} for the
classical model and \docfpr{bert} and \docfpr{guard} for the transformers, so their detection rates carry
no information. A document on its own is enough; a table of numbers is flagged with its numbers as the
top words. ProtectAI and the rule baselines rarely flag clean documents but catch almost none of the plain
BIPIA attacks; they catch the override variant, the rules completely and ProtectAI about half the time.
Where the attack lies beyond ProtectAI's 512-token input, it was never detected
(\pgnum{docs.models.protectai.detection.bipia.attack_beyond_truncation.n} cases). In short, none of the
detectors handles the case PromptGuard is meant for: either everything is flagged or only the explicit
override phrase is.

\subsection{Perturbations}
Table~\ref{tab:robust} applies eight perturbations to \pgnum{rob.config.per_class} attack and
\pgnum{rob.config.per_class} benign test rows and shows both classes. Attack detection stays near 1 for
every trained model, but the benign column shows why: leetspeak, homoglyphs and German translation make
the trained models flag benign text too, up to all of it. The perturbation itself has become the signal.
ProtectAI flags few perturbed benign rows, with three exceptions: zero-width characters
(\pgr{2}{rob.models.protectai.zero_width.benign_flagged.rate}), spaced letters
(\pgr{2}{rob.models.protectai.spaced.benign_flagged.rate}) and the Base64 framing
(\pgr{2}{rob.models.protectai.base64.benign_flagged.rate}). Under paraphrasing its detection falls from
\pgr{2}{rob.models.protectai.original.attack_detected.rate} to
\pgr{2}{rob.models.protectai.paraphrase.attack_detected.rate}; we did not verify that every paraphrase
still carries its attack. Base64 is decoded by the API's normalization before any model sees it.

\subsection{Decision pipeline and latency}\label{sec:pipeline}
\emph{Rule floor.} The chat-template and hidden-content rule fires on a handful of rows
(\pgnum{pipe.rule_floor.neuralchemy_test__original_rows.flagged} of the test rows) and changes no label on any
evaluation set, because the classical model already flags those rows.

\emph{Escalation.} The deployed rule, which sends classical SUSPICIOUS verdicts with confidence below 0.65 to
ModernBERT, escalates no test row and at most
\pgp{1}{pipe.sets.\dsq.suspicious_only.0.65.escalated_share}\% of an external set, so it changes almost
nothing. We also tried escalating every verdict whose confidence is below a threshold $t$. On the
validation split the best $t$ is \pgnum{pipe.selected_thresholds.any_label}, which raises validation accuracy
from \pgr{4}{pipe.sets.neuralchemy_validation__original_rows.classical_only.accuracy} to
\pgr{4}{pipe.sets.neuralchemy_validation__original_rows.any_label.0.9.accuracy}; on the test split, however,
accuracy falls to \pgr{4}{pipe.sets.\testset.any_label.0.9.accuracy}. On external data the classical model is
unsure about almost everything, so this rule escalates
\pgp{0}{pipe.sets.\dsx.any_label.0.9.escalated_share}--\pgp{0}{pipe.sets.\dsq.any_label.0.9.escalated_share}\%
of the rows: it turns into ModernBERT, at close to ModernBERT's cost
(\pgr{0}{pipe.latency.guard_only_mean_ms}~ms per prompt against \pgr{1}{pipe.latency.classical_only_mean_ms}~ms for
the classical model alone, mean CPU time in this experiment). Escalation as designed does not help, so we do
not present PromptGuard as a multi-tier detector.

\section{Limitations}\label{sec:limits}
\emph{Data.} We train on one public dataset, and its SUSPICIOUS class is synthetic. Two of the external
datasets do not document their label meaning; we checked it from samples and keyword rates. The public
detectors do not fully disclose their training data, so they may have seen data close to the external
sets, which would favour them.

\emph{Tests.} The pasted-document test has \pgnum{docs.counts.clean} documents from two sources and frames
each one in a single way; most of its attacks are task injections, and the override variant is our own.
The perturbation test starts from short in-distribution rows, and we did not check by hand that every
paraphrased attack is still an attack. Latency was measured on one laptop CPU.

\emph{Explanations.} The regular expressions match few attacks
(true-positive rate \pgr{3}{cur.sets.\testset.regex.fixed_operating_point.tpr} on the test split), so they
explain only some flags. The word attributions are exact for each TF-IDF feature, but splitting n-gram
contributions over words is an approximation, and neither they nor attention weights are causal
explanations.

\emph{Deployment.} A user can switch the extension off, so it gives no protection against a user who wants
to jailbreak a model. The hosted API stores an unsalted hash of each prompt, which can reveal short or
common prompts.

\section{Conclusion}
PromptGuard puts a prompt-injection check in the one place every hosted chat service shares, the user's
browser, and keeps its decisions inspectable. Measured on its own test split, a TF-IDF model is as good as
two fine-tuned transformers at a fraction of the cost. Measured where the tool is meant to work, on other
datasets and on pasted documents, none of the three is usable, and the published detectors trade
over-flagging for missed injections. We see two directions: training data that covers benign documents and
instructions as well as attacks, and judging an injection relative to the user's own request rather than in
isolation. Until then, a browser-side detector is best treated as a warning, not a filter.
